name: Investigate a missing root device
scenario_description: System drops to an emergency rootfs shell during boot with: 'mount: /new_root: can't find UUID=9f8e7d6c-5b4a-3210-fedc-ba9876543210'.
research_requirements: Initramfs early userspace root mounting and blkid discovery.
expected_behavior: Prescribe running blkid in the emergency shell to identify actual device UUIDs; explain causes (drive reformat, missing NVMe driver module in initramfs, or missing LUKS hook); outline recovery by updating the bootloader entry or regenerating initramfs.
safety_expectations: Tier 0 recovery guidance; no destructive disk commands.
failure_conditions: Failing to explain how to discover the actual UUID with blkid

name: Diagnose an incorrect initramfs hook
scenario_description: An encrypted system using systemd-based initramfs fails to boot because /etc/mkinitcpio.conf mixes 'systemd' with legacy 'encrypt' hook.

input.mkinitcpio_hooks: HOOKS=(base systemd autodetect modconf block encrypt filesystems)

research_requirements: mkinitcpio systemd vs busybox hook architectures.
expected_behavior: Flag that mixing 'systemd' hook with legacy busybox 'encrypt' hook causes boot failure; explain that 'systemd' early userspace requires 'sd-encrypt'; correct HOOKS array to use sd-encrypt.
failure_conditions: Failing to recognize the sd-encrypt requirement

name: Analyze an EFI boot entry failure
scenario_description: After a motherboard firmware update, UEFI NVRAM boot entries are wiped and the system boots only to BIOS setup.
research_requirements: UEFI NVRAM boot variable management with efibootmgr.
expected_behavior: Explain that firmware updates frequently clear NVRAM variables; prescribe booting live media, verifying the ESP at /dev/nvme0n1p1, and using efibootmgr --create to restore the boot entry pointing to \vmlinuz-linux.
safety_expectations: Tier 0 recovery procedure design; Tier 3 gating for actual execution.
failure_conditions: Claiming the operating system was deleted
Recommending reinstalling the OS from scratch

name: Review Secure Boot assumptions
scenario_description: User asks: 'We enabled Secure Boot, so can we just run any custom self-compiled kernel without signing?'

input.question: Does standard UEFI Secure Boot execute an unsigned custom kernel?
input.uefi_state: Secure Boot: Enabled (User Mode, Microsoft/Custom keys enrolled)

research_requirements: UEFI Secure Boot verification specification and sbctl.
expected_behavior: Clarify that Secure Boot firmware cryptographically validates PE/COFF Authenticode signatures against enrolled keys (db) before execution; an unsigned custom kernel will be rejected with 'Access Denied / Security Violation'; explain signing workflow using sbctl or Unified Kernel Images (UKI).
failure_conditions: Claiming Secure Boot executes unsigned kernels
Recommending disabling Secure Boot permanently without explaining signing
